goal: Close the ways a known-dangerous URL can slip past the safety filter, let people sign themselves up for an account, and let someone who is not signed in turn a long URL into a short link that expires after one month.
in_scope: Item 1: strengthen the check that stops a URL we know to be dangerous (denylisted host, or an internal address) from being turned into a short link, treating the two confirmed bypasses as examples of a weak check rather than as the complete list.
Item 1 (example): a host written with a trailing dot, e.g. https://malware.example.com./x, is recognised as the host that was blocked.
Item 1 (example): an address written as a plain number, e.g. http://2130706433/, is recognised as an internal address.
Item 1: a test that fails against the current code and demonstrates the weakness, written and shown before the fix, and kept in the suite afterwards.
Item 2: a way for a person to create their own account, then sign in with it and use the service exactly as an existing customer does.
Item 2: the same rules that already apply to how the service holds passwords apply to passwords chosen at sign-up.
Item 2: two people must not be able to end up with the same account name, however close together they try.
Item 3: an unauthenticated way to turn a long URL into a short link.
Item 3: a link created that way expires one month after it is created.

Item 3: such a link behaves like any other short link in every other respect — it redirects the same way, its clicks are counted the same way, and the same safety rules apply, including the filter from item 1.
Item 3: nobody owns such a link, so nobody can list it, change it, delete it, or see its numbers; holding the link is the whole of the holder's relationship with the service.
Item 3: the anonymous creation path is subject to the anti-abuse system the service already has.

Preserving the existing isolation model: an account created under item 2 is as isolated from other customers as the existing accounts are, and a link created under item 3 does not become a way to see anything other than itself.
Keeping the click path the priority: refusing a new anonymous link is preferred to serving a click slowly.
out_of_scope: Removing or changing the two hand-installed seeded accounts (explicitly deferred by the requester; tracked separately and depends on this landing first).
Designing a new anti-abuse or rate-limiting system from scratch; the existing one is to be used.
Password reset, password change, or account recovery — not mentioned in the requirement.
Account deletion or profile management — not mentioned.
Sign-out, token refresh, or token revocation — unchanged from the current build.
Any way for an anonymous link to later be claimed by, transferred to, or associated with an account.
Any listing, editing, deletion, or statistics surface for anonymous links, for anyone including staff.
Changing the expiry, target URL, or any other property of an anonymous link, including by its holder.
An admin endpoint or console for the threat denylist; adding hosts remains a migration.
A moderation queue or unblock path for abuse reports.
Any user interface; the deliverable is the HTTP API.
Changes to the existing authenticated link, click, abuse-report, and session endpoints beyond what items 1-3 require.
CAPTCHA, proof-of-work, email or phone challenges, or any new anti-abuse mechanism for anonymous creation.
Enumerating or auditing bypasses of the safety filter beyond making the check itself sound (the requester states more may exist).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Creating a link whose target host is a denylisted host written with a trailing dot (e.g. https://malware.example.com./x) is refused with 422 url_rejected, the same as the host written without the trailing dot.
Creating a link whose target host is an internal address written in a non-dotted-quad numeric form (e.g. http://2130706433/) is refused with 422 url_rejected, the same as the equivalent dotted form.
The test suite contains tests covering AC1 and AC2 that fail against the pre-change code and pass after the change, and those tests remain in the suite after the fix.
An unauthenticated caller can create a new account by supplying an account name and password, and receives a success response.
After creating an account, signing in with those credentials succeeds and returns a session token, and that token is accepted by every endpoint an existing customer's token is accepted by.

A second attempt to create an account with an account name that already exists is refused, and when two such attempts are made concurrently exactly one succeeds and the other is refused; the stored data never contains two accounts with the same account name.
A password supplied at sign-up is never stored or returned in recoverable form; the stored representation is produced by the same password-holding mechanism the existing accounts use.

A customer created via sign-up cannot see, modify, or delete another customer's link: requests naming another customer's code answer 404 not_found, and the sign-up customer's link list contains only their own links.
An unauthenticated caller can create a short link from a long URL and receives the code and short URL in the response, with no credentials supplied.
A link created anonymously has an expiry one month after its creation time, and after that point requests for its code answer 404 not_found.
Following an anonymously created code returns the same redirect response (status, Location, cache headers) as an owner-created link, and its clicks are counted by the same mechanism.
An anonymous creation request whose target is denylisted, internal, or otherwise refused by the safety filter — including the AC1 and AC2 forms — is refused with 422 url_rejected.

No caller, signed in or not, can list, modify, delete, or read the click count of an anonymously created link: such requests answer 404 not_found, and the code never appears in any customer's link list.

Anonymous creation is rate limited by the service's existing rate-limiting mechanism: exceeding the limit returns 429 rate_limited with a non-zero Retry-After, and the anonymous path cannot be used to bypass the limits that apply to authenticated creation.

Under conditions in which the service refuses new link creation today (e.g. a dependency it needs is unavailable), anonymous creation is refused with the existing error response while the click path continues to serve redirects.
The two seeded accounts still exist and can still sign in after the change.
Every endpoint and behaviour documented before this change, other than those altered by AC1-AC16, answers as documented; the existing test suite passes unchanged.

constraints: A change to the live service in this repository, not a rebuild; the code here is what runs in production.
Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.5, PostgreSQL as system of record, Redis for cache, click counters and rate-limit buckets — as before.
The deliverable is the HTTP API; there is still no UI.
The failing test for item 1 must be produced and visible before the fix, and retained afterwards.
Ordering stated by the requester: item 1 (filter bypass) matters most, then item 2 (sign-up), then item 3 (anonymous creation).
The existing anti-abuse system must govern the anonymous creation path; a path that ignores it is stated to be worse than not shipping the feature.
The existing error envelope and status-code contract (invalid_request / unauthorized / not_found / url_rejected / rate_limited / service_unavailable, no 403, no 410) applies to any new endpoint.
The API contract in artifacts/openapi.yaml is the machine-readable contract for the service and must continue to describe it.
The schema is owned by versioned Flyway migrations; ddl-auto is validate.
service/src/main/resources/application.yml is a protected path in the pipeline; changes to connectivity or HTTP exposure require a human.
Ambiguity retained as given: 'account name' vs the existing email-keyed sign-in is not resolved here; the requirement says only that two people must not end up with the same account name.
Ambiguity retained as given: 'expires one month after it is created' is not resolved against the existing 30-day default TTL.
Ambiguity retained as given: 'the same rules that already apply to us holding passwords' is not restated in implementation terms.
Ambiguity retained as given: which key the existing anti-abuse system should use for an unauthenticated creator (there is no customer id) is not resolved.
non_functional: The click path keeps its existing priority and latency behaviour: degradation is spent on refusing new links, never on serving clicks.
Security: the safety filter must resist equivalent-form evasion generally, not only the two confirmed forms.
Security: a customer's links remain invisible to every other customer; existing indistinguishability of not_found responses is preserved so no endpoint reveals whether a code exists.
Security: an unauthenticated endpoint that writes to the database must not become an unmetered storage-burn vector.
Availability: existing behaviour when Redis or PostgreSQL is degraded is unchanged.
Operability: new behaviour is observable through the existing health, metrics and logging surfaces, and any new limits are configurable in the existing style.
